title: Fibonacci Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the nth Fibonacci number with F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
Idea: In fib(n), start a=0,b=1; repeat n times replacing them with b and a+b, then return a.
Technique and why it applies: An iterative recurrence computes each Fibonacci value once and avoids recursive call overhead.
Invariant: At the start of each iteration, a and b hold consecutive Fibonacci numbers F(i) and F(i+1).
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; n=1 returns one; larger n advances the pair n times. Python integers grow as needed, though very large outputs require more bit storage.
Complexity: O(n) arithmetic steps and O(1) stored integers, excluding the growing bit length of Fibonacci values.
complexity_reason: The loop performs n pair updates and retains only a and b.

title: Fibonacci Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Return Fibonacci number n, where F(0)=0 and F(1)=1.
Idea: Initialize a=0,b=1; for each i below n, compute next=a+b, shift a to b and b to next, then return a.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative recurrence reuses two consecutive values instead of building a table or recursive call tree.
Invariant: After i iterations, a and b represent F(i) and F(i+1), so the final a is F(n).
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; n=1 returns one; Java int arithmetic overflows for sufficiently large n, although standard constraints fit the required return type.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space because each iteration does fixed work with three int variables.
complexity_reason: The for loop executes n times and retains only a, b, and next.

title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the leftmost value on the last row of a nonempty binary tree.
Idea: Queue root, repeatedly remove the front node, enqueue its right child before its left child, and return the final removed node's value.
Technique and why it applies: Right-first breadth-first traversal visits nodes level by level but places rightmost nodes first within each level.
Invariant: Because each deeper level is processed after the previous one, the last node removed belongs to the deepest level and is its leftmost node under this queue order.
Edge cases: A single-node tree returns the root value; a right-skewed tree returns its deepest node; root is guaranteed nonempty. Enqueuing right before left is essential to make the final node the leftmost of the bottom row.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space, where n is node count and w is maximum queue width.
complexity_reason: Every tree node is enqueued and removed once, with the queue holding at most one level's pending nodes.

title: Find Bottom Left Tree Value
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the leftmost node value in the bottom row of a nonempty binary tree.
Idea: Add root to q, repeatedly remove a node, enqueue its right child before its left child, and finally return node.val from the last removal.
Technique and why it applies: Right-first level-order traversal reverses within-level processing so the last visited node at maximum depth is the leftmost.
Invariant: The queue remains ordered by depth, and right-before-left ordering makes the last node of the deepest level its leftmost value.
Edge cases: A single-node tree returns its root; a right-only chain returns its deepest node; root is guaranteed non-null. ArrayDeque cannot accept null children, so each child is checked before enqueueing.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space for n nodes and maximum width w.
complexity_reason: Each node is added to and removed from q once, and the queue holds pending nodes from nearby levels.

title: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest node value at each binary-tree depth from root downward.
Idea: Use BFS; at each level initialize best to negative infinity, pop the current queue size, update best from node.val, enqueue children, and append best.
Technique and why it applies: Level-order traversal isolates each depth, allowing a maximum to be computed without mixing rows.
Invariant: The queue-size snapshot defines the current level, and best is the largest value among exactly those nodes.
Edge cases: A null root returns []; a negative-only level still works because best starts at negative infinity; a single node yields a one-item result.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space for n nodes and maximum width w, plus one result per level.
complexity_reason: Each node is removed once and its children are enqueued once, while q stores at most a level's frontier.

title: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row
notes:
Task and constraints: Return one maximum value for each binary-tree level, ordered top to bottom.
Idea: Return an empty list for null root; otherwise process q.size() nodes per level, update best from each n.val, enqueue children, and append best.
Technique and why it applies: Breadth-first search processes a fixed depth at a time so its maximum can be recorded independently.
Invariant: The saved size bounds the inner loop to the current level even as children are added to q.
Edge cases: Null root returns an empty list; a level of negative values is handled by Integer.MIN_VALUE; a single-node tree returns its value.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(w) queue space, where w is maximum width, plus O(h) output values for h levels.
complexity_reason: The queue processes each node once and the inner loop performs one maximum comparison per node.

title: Detect Capital
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when a word is all uppercase, all lowercase, or capitalized only at its first letter.
Idea: Evaluate word.isupper(), word.islower(), or word.istitle(); any true condition accepts the word.
Technique and why it applies: Built-in string predicates check the three permitted capitalization patterns directly.
Invariant: The result is true if at least one complete-word capitalization predicate recognizes the input's case pattern.
Edge cases: 'USA' and 'leetcode' pass; 'Google' passes title case; 'FlaG' fails. Python title-case behavior treats word boundaries and nonletters according to str.istitle().
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from implementation details, since the predicates scan the word.
complexity_reason: The three string predicates inspect characters of word, with no collections or loops created by the method.

title: Detect Capital
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether word is all uppercase, all lowercase, or uppercase only at the first character.
Idea: Compare word with its uppercase and lowercase forms; otherwise require an uppercase first character and compare the suffix with its lowercase form.
Technique and why it applies: String-case comparisons validate the allowed patterns without counting uppercase characters manually.
Invariant: The return expression accepts exactly when one of the full-string case checks or the first-character-plus-lowercase-suffix check succeeds.
Edge cases: 'USA' and 'leetcode' pass; 'Google' passes; 'FlaG' fails. The implementation assumes word is nonempty because it accesses charAt(0), and Java case conversion can depend on Unicode rules.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) temporary string space for case-converted copies and the suffix.
complexity_reason: The method constructs or compares a constant number of strings whose lengths are proportional to word.

title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence I
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest uncommon subsequence length of strings a and b, or -1 if no such subsequence exists.
Idea: findLUSlength returns -1 if a equals b; otherwise it returns the greater of their lengths.
Technique and why it applies: When strings differ, the longer entire string cannot be a subsequence of the shorter, so its full length is optimal.
Invariant: The equality test separates the only impossible case; for unequal strings, at least one full input string is uncommon to the other.
Edge cases: Equal strings return -1; unequal lengths return the longer length; unequal strings of equal length return that common length. No character-level subsequence check is needed.
Complexity: O(n+m) time for equality comparison and O(1) extra space for lengths, where n and m are the string lengths.
complexity_reason: The method compares the strings once and computes the maximum of their two lengths.

title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence I
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest uncommon subsequence of a and b, or -1 when none exists.
Idea: Return -1 when a.equals(b); otherwise return Math.max(a.length(), b.length()).
Technique and why it applies: For unequal strings, the longer complete string cannot be a subsequence of the shorter, making it an uncommon subsequence.
Invariant: The equality branch handles identical strings, while inequality guarantees at least one full input is not a subsequence of the other.
Edge cases: Equal strings return -1; unequal strings of equal length return that length; different lengths return the larger length. Java compares string contents with equals rather than reference identity.
Complexity: O(n+m) time for equality comparison and O(1) auxiliary space for length values.
complexity_reason: The method performs one string equality comparison and constant-time length and maximum operations after it.

title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence II
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest string in strs that is not a subsequence of any other string in the array.
Idea: Sort indices by descending string length; for each candidate, call is_sub against every other string and return the first candidate passing all checks.
Technique and why it applies: Descending-length search finds the optimal answer as soon as a candidate is uncommon, while a two-pointer subsequence test checks containment.
Invariant: is_sub advances its pointer in a only when the current character of b matches, so reaching len(a) proves a is a subsequence of b.
Edge cases: An empty strs returns -1; duplicate identical strings disqualify each other; longer candidates are checked first. The same index is skipped, allowing a unique string to qualify against itself exclusion.
Complexity: O(n²*L) worst-case time for n strings of maximum length L, plus O(n log n) sorting; O(n) index storage.
complexity_reason: The code sorts n indices and may compare each candidate against n strings, scanning each target string during is_sub.

title: Longest Uncommon Subsequence II
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest string not contained as a subsequence in any other entry of strs.
Idea: Build idx with all positions, sort indices by descending string length, then test each candidate using isSub against every other index and return the first valid length.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting candidates by length ensures the first uncommon subsequence found is as long as possible.
Invariant: isSub advances through b and increments i only when the next character of a matches, returning true only when all of a is consumed.
Edge cases: An empty array returns -1; duplicate strings disqualify each other; the same index is excluded from comparison. Java sorting uses an Integer index array, and equal-length ties can be returned in either order if valid.
Complexity: O(n²*L) worst-case time plus O(n log n) sorting, and O(n) index storage plus O(L) temporary character arrays.
complexity_reason: The method sorts n boxed indices and can call isSub for each ordered candidate against n strings.

title: Continuous Subarray Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a contiguous subarray of length at least two sums to a multiple of k.
Idea: Store the first index for each prefix remainder, beginning with remainder 0 at index -1; for each x update total and use total itself when k==0 or total%abs(k) otherwise.
Technique and why it applies: Equal prefix remainders imply the intervening sum is divisible by k; earliest indices maximize the available subarray length.
Invariant: first[r] is the earliest prefix index with remainder r, so a repeated remainder forms a qualifying subarray when the index gap is at least two.
Edge cases: A repeated remainder one index later is too short; k=0 requires a zero-sum subarray; negative k is normalized with abs. Python integers avoid overflow.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space for the first-index dictionary.
complexity_reason: The loop processes nums once and stores only the first index seen for each distinct prefix remainder.

title: Continuous Subarray Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Check for a length-at-least-two subarray whose sum is divisible by k.
Idea: Use first to store the earliest index for each prefix sum or remainder; update long sum, use sum directly when k==0 and sum%mod otherwise, and test repeated keys for an index gap of at least two.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix remainder equality identifies divisible subarray sums, while retaining the first occurrence ensures the longest possible gap for each remainder.
Invariant: first maps each encountered remainder to its earliest prefix index, so later matches can be tested by subtracting indices.
Edge cases: A repeated key with gap one is not enough; k=0 checks equal prefix sums; Math.abs((long)k) handles Integer.MIN_VALUE. Long sum avoids cumulative int overflow.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space for the HashMap of first prefix indices.
complexity_reason: The single pass updates a long prefix sum and performs expected constant-time map lookups for each element.

title: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest dictionary word obtainable by deleting characters from s, breaking length ties lexicographically.
Idea: For each dictionary word, is_sub scans s and advances a pointer when the next required character matches; update ans for a longer match or a lexicographically smaller equal-length match.
Technique and why it applies: A two-pointer subsequence test checks whether each candidate can be formed without rearranging s, and explicit tie-breaking selects the required answer.
Invariant: The pointer in w advances only on a matching character from s, preserving character order and proving the candidate is a subsequence when all its characters are consumed.
Edge cases: An empty dictionary returns ''; an empty candidate qualifies; equal-length valid words choose the lexicographically smaller one. Python string comparison determines lexicographic order.
Complexity: O(D*S + total dictionary length) time and O(1) auxiliary space per check, where D is dictionary size and S=len(s).
complexity_reason: Each candidate may scan all of s, so the loop performs O(D*S) character checks and retains only ans and a pointer.

title: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting
notes:
Task and constraints: Choose the longest dictionary word that is a subsequence of s, breaking ties by lexicographically smallest text.
Idea: For each w, call isSub(w,s); replace ans if w is longer or if equal length and w.compareTo(ans)<0.
Technique and why it applies: The two-pointer test preserves order while the comparison rule directly implements longest-first and lexical tie-breaking.
Invariant: isSub advances its index in w only when a character of s matches, so success means all of w appeared in order.
Edge cases: An empty dictionary returns ''; an empty candidate is a subsequence; equal-length valid words use compareTo to select the lexical minimum. Java compares strings by UTF-16 code units.
Complexity: O(D*S + total candidate lengths) time and O(1) extra space per check, where D is dictionary size and S=len(s).
complexity_reason: The code may scan s once for each dictionary entry and stores only the current answer.

title: Contiguous Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a contiguous binary subarray with equal numbers of zeros and ones.
Idea: Track balance by adding one for 1 and minus one otherwise; first stores the earliest index for each balance, and best updates from repeated balances.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix balance converts equal-zero/one subarrays into intervals whose net balance is zero.
Invariant: The same balance at indices i and j means the values between them contain equal numbers of zeros and ones; first retains the longest such interval.
Edge cases: An empty array returns zero; [0,1] returns two; all zeros never repeat a balance after the initial seed in a way yielding a positive balanced interval. The code treats every non-one value as zero.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space for first-seen balance indices.
complexity_reason: The loop updates one balance per value and stores only the first index for each distinct balance.

title: Contiguous Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the longest contiguous segment with equal counts of zeros and ones.
Idea: Initialize first with balance 0 at index -1; update bal by plus one for 1 and minus one otherwise, then use repeated balances to extend best.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-sum hashing finds zero-sum intervals without checking every possible subarray.
Invariant: A repeated bal means the interval between its first occurrence and current index has equal numbers of zeros and ones.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; [0,1] yields length two; the initial -1 index permits balanced subarrays starting at index zero. Values are assumed binary, as all non-ones are treated as zero.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) extra space for the map of earliest balance indices.
complexity_reason: Each array value updates bal once and causes one HashMap lookup, with at most n+1 stored balances.

title: Beautiful Arrangement
notes:
Task and constraints: Count permutations of values 1..n where each position i is divisible by its value x or vice versa.
Idea: dfs(pos) tries every unused x satisfying x%pos==0 or pos%x==0, marks used[x], adds recursive completions, and unmarks x after backtracking.
Technique and why it applies: Constraint-guided backtracking constructs valid permutations one position at a time and skips values that cannot fit the current position.
Invariant: At entry to dfs(pos), positions before pos are assigned distinct values, and used exactly marks those values.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one; values failing both divisibility tests are skipped; after each recursive branch used[x] is reset so another permutation can use x. The search assumes n is positive.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n!) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the used array and recursion depth.
complexity_reason: The DFS explores unused candidates at each position, with recursion depth n and one boolean slot per value.

title: Beautiful Arrangement
notes:
Task and constraints: Count valid arrangements of 1..n where each position and its assigned value divide one another.
Idea: Set n and used, then dfs(pos) tries each unused x satisfying x%pos==0 or pos%x==0, marks it, accumulates completions, and clears it after recursion.
Technique and why it applies: Backtracking builds permutations while divisibility constraints prune invalid choices at each position.
Invariant: At dfs(pos), every earlier position has one distinct selected value and used records exactly those selections.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one; nondivisible candidates are skipped; resetting used[x] after recursion is necessary to explore other arrangements. int counts rely on the problem's small n bound.
Complexity: Worst-case O(n!) time and O(n) auxiliary space for used and the recursive call stack.
complexity_reason: The recursive search can explore permutations of n values and stores n flags plus at most n stack frames.
